from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Primes act as the atoms of arithmetic.",
            "Numbers grow, yet primes become rarer.",
            "Prime density follows 1/ln(x) approximately.",
            "Visualizing prime thinning in a grid.",
            "[Asset: PrimeGrid_10x10] shows this clearly."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Prerequisite: The Nature of Primes", lecture_lines)
        
        # Helper to get primes up to 100
        def is_prime(n):
            if n < 2: return False
            for i in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1):
                if n % i == 0: return False
            return True

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FF4500")
        dots = VGroup(*[Dot(radius=0.1) for _ in range(100)])
        self.place_in_area(dots, "A1", "F6", scale_factor=0.5)
        self.play(Create(dots))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#00CED1")
        # Just hold
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#FFD700")
        primes = [i+1 for i in range(100) if is_prime(i+1)]
        non_primes = [i+1 for i in range(100) if not is_prime(i+1)]
        
        prime_group = VGroup(*[dots[i-1] for i in primes])
        self.play(prime_group.animate.set_color("#FF4500"))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.lecture[3].set_color("#ADFF2F")
        non_prime_group = VGroup(*[dots[i-1] for i in non_primes])
        self.play(non_prime_group.animate.set_color("#00CED1"))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.lecture[4].set_color("#FF69B4")
        self.play(FadeOut(non_prime_group))
        self.wait(2)

class Section2Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = ["Primes appear random, but are not.", "Dirichlet's Theorem proves deeper ordered structure.", "Infinitely many primes exist in arithmetic progressions."]
        self.setup_layout("Prime Patterns & Dirichlet’s Theorem", lecture_lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color("#FFFFFF"))
        mod_table = Table(
            [[str(i) for i in range(1, 5)], [str(i+4) for i in range(1, 5)]],
            col_labels=[Text("n=0"), Text("n=1"), Text("n=2"), Text("n=3")]
        ).scale(0.3)
        self.place_at_grid(mod_table, 'B2', scale_factor=0.6)
        mod_table.set_color("#FFFF00")
        self.play(Create(mod_table))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#FF4500"))
        progression = MathTex("a + nd").set_color("#FF4500")
        self.place_at_grid(progression, 'D3', scale_factor=1.2)
        self.play(Write(progression))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#00CED1"))
        inf_primes = Text("Infinitely many!").set_color("#00CED1")
        self.place_at_grid(inf_primes, 'E4', scale_factor=0.8)
        self.play(GrowFromCenter(inf_primes))
        self.wait(1)

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Approximating Pi via Prime Distribution", [
            "Primes bridge number theory and geometry.",
            "Random coprime integers define 6/π squared.",
            "Prime properties help estimate pi's value."
        ])
        
        # Animations
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FFFFFF")
        title_obj = Text("Approximating Pi", font_size=32, color="#FFFFFF")
        self.place_at_grid(title_obj, 'A3')
        self.play(Write(title_obj))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FF4500")
        axes = Axes(x_range=[0, 10, 2], y_range=[0, 1, 0.2], axis_config={"include_numbers": False})
        curve = axes.plot(lambda x: 0.607, color="#FF4500")
        graph_group = VGroup(axes, curve)
        self.place_in_area(graph_group, 'B1', 'D6', scale_factor=0.6)
        self.play(Create(graph_group))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#00CED1")
        pi_approx = MathTex(r"\\pi \approx \sqrt{\frac{6}{P}}", color="#00CED1")
        self.place_at_grid(pi_approx, 'E3', scale_factor=1.2)
        
        dot = Dot(color="#FFFF00")
        self.place_at_grid(dot, 'F3')
        
        self.play(Write(pi_approx), FadeIn(dot))
        self.wait(2)

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Prime distribution reveals deep mathematical unity.",
            "Dirichlet and PNT link primes to constants.",
            "Pi appears within prime sequence structure."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Synthesis: The Harmony of Numbers", lecture_lines)
        
        # --- Create Visuals ---
        # Represent primes as dots for the "Prime Grid"
        primes = VGroup(*[Dot(radius=0.05, color=BLUE) for _ in range(25)])
        primes.arrange_in_grid(5, 5, buff=0.2)
        self.place_at_grid(primes, 'C3', scale_factor=1.2)
        
        # Pi representation
        pi_symbol = MathTex(r"\pi", color=RED).scale(2)
        self.place_at_grid(pi_symbol, 'C3', scale_factor=0.5)
        pi_symbol.set_opacity(0)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(primes))
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.play(primes.animate.set_color(PURPLE))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[2].set_color(WHITE)
        self.play(
            FadeOut(primes),
            FadeIn(pi_symbol),
            pi_symbol.animate.set_color(YELLOW).scale(3)
        )
        self.wait(2)

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Nature of Primes
sections.content: Define primes as the 'atoms' of arithmetic. Introduce the Prime Number Theorem (PNT) visually: as numbers grow, primes become sparser, following a density of approximately 1/ln(x).
sections.example: Visualizing a 10x10 grid of numbers where primes are highlighted in neon blue, showing the thinning population density as we reach higher ranges.

sections.title: Prime Patterns & Dirichlet’s Theorem
sections.content: Explain that while primes seem random, Dirichlet’s Theorem proves they aren't entirely chaotic. It states that for any two coprime integers a and d, there are infinitely many primes of the form a + nd.
sections.example: A 'Number Bus' animation: If we look at numbers ending in 1, 3, 7, or 9 (the 'last digit' logic), a character like 'Detective Prime' observes that these 'lanes' of numbers will never run out of prime passengers.

sections.title: Approximating Pi via Prime Distribution
sections.content: Bridge the gap between number theory and geometry. Show how the probability of two random integers being coprime is 6/π². Use this to demonstrate how prime properties allow us to estimate the value of π.
sections.example: An animation of a 'Robot Gardener' planting random seeds; the ratio of seeds that don't share any factors (coprime) eventually forms a pattern that converges toward the value 6/π².

sections.title: Synthesis: The Harmony of Numbers
sections.content: Summarize that the distribution of primes (governed by Dirichlet and the PNT) is intimately linked to the fundamental constants of the universe, like π, illustrating a deep, underlying mathematical unity.
sections.example: A final 5-second visualization where the 'Prime Grid' from Section 1 rotates and transforms into a circle, revealing the π constant hidden within the structure of the prime sequence.
